# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Clinical Review

The transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (TV-ICD) is a well-established therapy for the prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD) [1]. However, TV-ICD systems are associated with significant acute and long-term complications, primarily related to the presence of endovascular leads, including lead fracture, venous thrombosis, systemic infection, and cardiac perforation [2]. To address these drawbacks, the subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed [1, 3]. By placing the entire system, including the generator and lead, in the subcutaneous space, the S-ICD avoids the vascular system and the heart entirely, preserving venous access and minimizing endovascular risks [3, 4].

### System Screening and Vector Selection

Because the S-ICD utilizes far-field electrocardiogram (ECG) sensing, it lacks the near-field resolution of traditional transvenous leads. This makes the system susceptible to cardiac oversensing, particularly of T-waves (T-wave oversensing, or TWO), which is a major cause of inappropriate shocks [4]. To identify suitable candidates, patients must undergo pre-implantation ECG screening using manual or automated systems [5]. This screening evaluates the QRS-to-T wave ratio across three sensing vectors in both supine and standing positions [5, 6]. Only patients with at least one acceptable sensing vector are eligible for S-ICD implantation [6].

### Clinical Efficacy and Real-World Evidence

The initial efficacy and safety of S-ICD therapy were demonstrated in the landmark Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) trial [2]. This was soon supported by real-world registries, such as the Evaluation of Factors Impacting Clinical Outcome and Cost Effectiveness of the S-ICD (EFFORTLESS) registry [4, 7, 8]. The S-ICD Post-Approval Study (PAS) further demonstrated high conversion rates of induced and spontaneous ventricular fibrillation, with safety profiles comparable to TV-ICDs [9]. Meta-analyses comparing S-ICD to TV-ICD have consistently shown similar rates of successful sudden cardiac death termination, with the S-ICD providing a significant reduction in lead-related complications, though early S-ICD generations had a higher incidence of inappropriate shocks [10, 11]. The clinical utility of S-ICDs has also been demonstrated in vulnerable subpopulations, including patients with congestive heart failure and end-stage renal disease [12].

### Algorithmic Solutions for Inappropriate Shocks

Inappropriate shocks represent a historically significant clinical challenge in S-ICD patients [4]. Early systems relied on basic sensing algorithms that occasionally struggled to differentiate between ventricular tachyarrhythmias and supraventricular tachycardias or TWO [13, 14]. Modern S-ICD programming utilizes sophisticated dual-zone detection (incorporating conditional shock zones) and advanced discrimination algorithms to prevent inappropriate therapies [4, 14]. Additionally, the introduction of the "SMART Pass" high-pass filter software has significantly reduced TWO-related shocks by filtering out low-frequency T-wave signals while maintaining appropriate ventricular sensing [15, 16]. Refinements in implantation techniques, such as the two-incision technique and serratus anterior plane blocks, have further reduced early post-operative discomfort and complications [17].

### Head-to-Head Trials and Guidelines

The clinical evidence base for the S-ICD has matured through landmark randomized controlled trials. The PRAETORIAN trial, the first randomized head-to-head comparison of S-ICD and TV-ICD systems, met its primary endpoint of non-inferiority for the composite outcome of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [18, 19]. While lead-related complications were significantly more common in the TV-ICD group, inappropriate shocks were more frequent in the S-ICD group, emphasizing the ongoing need for modern programming [18]. The subsequent UNTOUCHED trial proved that utilizing contemporary programming, including higher rate cutoffs and the SMART Pass filter, resulted in exceptionally low inappropriate shock rates in primary prevention patients with low ejection fractions, comparable to those of contemporary TV-ICDs [20]. More recently, the ATLAS trial demonstrated that S-ICD implantation dramatically reduced lead-related complications without a significant increase in inappropriate shocks [21].

Based on this robust body of evidence, current guidelines from the American Heart Association (AHA), American College of Cardiology (ACC), Heart Rhythm Society (HRS), and European Society of Cardiology (ESC) recommend the S-ICD as a Class I or IIa alternative to TV-ICDs in patients who do not have an indication for bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), or anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP) [22-24].

### Limitations and Modular Systems

Despite these clinical advancements, the lack of pacing capabilities remains the primary limitation of the S-ICD. This prevents its use in patients requiring pacing for bradycardia, CRT, or ATP to painlessly terminate monomorphic ventricular tachycardia [24, 25]. To address this gap, recent research has focused on modular cardiac rhythm management systems. These integrate an S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker (LCP) [26]. Leadless pacemakers and S-ICDs have been successfully co-implanted, and clinical evaluations show that they can safely communicate wirelessly to deliver ATP and post-shock pacing [27, 28]. This modular paradigm preserves the extravascular benefits of the S-ICD while adding essential pacing features [28]. As S-ICD technology continues to evolve, improving battery longevity [29] and verifying its safety in specific demographics like the elderly [30] will remain key clinical goals.
